newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU reacts cautiously to U.S. internet trade plan.
newsitem.headline: EU reacts cautiously to U.S. internet trade plan.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday welcomed proposals by U.S. president Bill Clinton for a global internet free-trade zone, saying many of his suggestions mirrored the EU's own initiatives.

Peter Guilford, spokesman for European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, told Reuters that at first sight Clinton's proposals looked interesting, but the whole concept clearly needed a great deal of further study.
"A lot of the issues are already being discussed," Guilford said. "But what exactly is a free-trade zone on the internet and does it take us further than where we are today?"
Clinton said in Washington on Tuesday that he wanted the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to begin work on establishing a free-trade zone for internet commerce within the year.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky later said she hoped to start with a basic group of countries -- including the EU -- to secure agreement on a laissez-faire policy on internet commerce and build global support from there.
"Let's find the critical mass of countries who will be the pace setters, the rest will follow," Barshefsky said.
Guilford said the Commission would be very willing to meet officials from the U.S. and other nations to discuss the issues and looked forward to meaningful contacts on the matter.

In April the Commission published a paper entitled "A European Initiative in Electronic Commerce" which sought to encourage growth in the industry while ensuring it remained unfettered by tariffs and taxes.

The Commission's paper, however, envisaged completing an industry review establishing regulatory frameworks by the end of the century, as opposed to Clinton's call for a global deal to be in place within a year.

Barshefsky said that much of the foundation for the internet commerce policy has already been set. The global agreement on information techonologies reached at a December meeting of WTO ministers eliminates import tariffs on many of the technologies used to access the interenet.
The United States and its trading partners have already agreed on a second round of information technology talks to address other trade barriers. Those talks are to begin in October.
A WTO agreement reached earlier this year that opens up telecommunications markets around the world to more foreign competition will help consumers access the the internet, Barshefsky said.

"Full and proper implementation of that deal will resolve all current market access issues with respect to accessing the internet, with respect to investment, with respect to ownership rights, with respect to non-discriminatory treatment," Barshefsky said.
She said that many of the issues that are involved in the internet initiative are being addressed in a number of international trade forums.
Clinton said he was also directing Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin to negotiate agreements to prevent new discriminatory taxes in electronic commerce.

U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley and Ira Magaziner, who headed development of the administration's Internet policy, will lead a delegation to Europe later this month to outline the U.S. vision for international electronic commerce.
